name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt a **single, unified "content gate"**—a 5-second duration filter applied *before* semantic checks—across all creative agents. This is the fastest way to cut noise without slowing down production.

**Why:** A 5-second gate catches empty or placeholder clips early, reducing wasted processing time for downstream semantic analysis. It’s simpler than debating thresholds and forces agents to deliver *something* usable immediately.

**Trade-off:** We accept a small risk of discarding ultra-short but high-impact clips (e.g., punchy 3-second hooks). The upside—faster iteration and cleaner pipelines—outweighs this.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk in Reel’s 5-second gate is that it still conflates duration with quality—empty clips get cut, but a 5-second clip could still be semantically hollow or misaligned. A better alternative is to pair the gate with a **real-time semantic confidence score** (e.g., 10% threshold) *before* duration checks, so we filter noise without discarding potential gems. Settle it by running a 2-week A/B test: compare the current gate alone vs. the combined filter, measuring downstream rework and semantic accuracy.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Run a blind 30-day A/B test between (A) the 5-second duration gate first, then 30% semantic relevance, and (B) the 5-second gate first, then 10% semantic confidence score—both applied before any transcode checks.

**Why:** The 10% semantic confidence score catches semantically hollow clips the 30% relevance threshold misses, but it risks over-filtering creative edges. The test will show if the trade-off in lost novelty outweighs the gain in semantic precision.

**Who:** Scriv owns the semantic scoring logic; Reel owns the gate implementation and A/B framework.
[dispatched 2 workers: worker-3167, worker-8628 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 30-day A/B test conflates two variables—duration gate vs. semantic confidence—so it won’t isolate which filter actually improves quality. Instead, run a 7-day head-to-head on the same 10k clips: one side gets the 5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance, the other gets the 5-second gate + 10% semantic confidence, both measured by human reviewers blind to the variant. The artifact is the review data showing which filter cuts noise fastest without killing good clips.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance threshold** as the default filter for all creative agents, with no A/B test.

**Why:** The 30% semantic threshold is stricter than 10%, catching more misaligned or hollow clips early without adding complexity. The trade-off is rejecting some borderline-good clips, but that’s better than wasting resources on low-value content. This is the fastest way to enforce quality at scale.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 30% semantic threshold risks over-filtering: it may reject clips that are *just* below the bar but still usable for downstream edits, wasting creative effort. A better alternative is to keep the 5-second gate but add a *lightweight* semantic check (e.g., 10%) *only* for clips that pass duration—this isolates the value of semantic filtering without locking in a rigid threshold. Settle it with a 7-day A/B test on 10k clips, measuring downstream edit time and final output quality.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 10% semantic confidence score** as the default filter for all creative agents.

This balances speed and quality: the 5-second gate cuts obvious noise early, while the 10% semantic score catches hollow or misaligned clips without over-filtering. The trade-off is accepting slightly more false positives—some usable clips may slip through—but this keeps production moving faster than stricter thresholds.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 10% semantic gate still lets through clips that are *just* coherent but irrelevant—wasting downstream edits on material that doesn’t serve the final output. A better alternative is to run a 14-day A/B test between (A) 5-second + 10% semantic and (B) 5-second + 10% semantic *plus* a lightweight human spot-check on the top 5% of rejected clips—this isolates whether the semantic score alone is sufficient or if human judgment closes the gap. The lead for this test should be the Creative Ops team.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance threshold** as the default filter for all creative agents, with no A/B test.

**Why:** The 30% threshold is stricter, catching more misaligned or hollow clips early—reducing wasted downstream edits. The trade-off is rejecting some usable clips, but that’s preferable to letting noise slip through.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 30% semantic threshold risks over-filtering: it may reject clips that are *just* below the bar but still usable for downstream edits, wasting creative effort. A better alternative is to run a 7-day head-to-head on the same 10k clips: one side gets the 5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance, the other gets the 5-second gate + 10% semantic relevance *plus* a lightweight human review for borderline cases. The artifact is a 7-day report showing reject rates and downstream edit waste.
